blocks.text: 7.2.4. Generic Methods in Enums
The payments service reads its settings through an enum, and `RetryPolicy` takes its limit from it when the service starts:
The service starts and passes its health check. The first payment that needs a retry fails:

Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer (java.lang.String and java.lang.Integer are in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap')
	at RetryPolicy.attemptsLeft(RetryPolicy.java:12)
	at Opening.main(Opening.java:8)
`RetryPolicy` hasn't changed in a year. The bug is in `Setting.find`, which `RetryPolicy` calls, a generic method on an enum, and the stack trace doesn't mention it.
An Enum Can't Take a Type Parameter, but Its Methods Can, and Each Call Picks T
An enum declaration can't be generic:
JEP 301 proposed generic enums and was withdrawn; unit 7.2.2 covers the replacements. A method of an enum can still declare its own type parameter. This is the `Setting` that `RetryPolicy` uses:
With `props` holding `http.retries=3`, which of these lines compile?

Integer retries = Setting.RETRIES.read(props);
String text = Setting.RETRIES.read(props);

Both do. `T` belongs to each call, not to the constant: the compiler infers it from what the caller assigns the result to, so `T` is `Integer` in the first line and `String` in the second. Nothing ties `RETRIES` to `Integer`, because a constant has no type argument to carry it; only a typed key (unit 7.2.2) can make that promise.
An Unchecked Cast Checks Nothing Where It Is Written
javac compiles `Setting` with a note to recompile with `-Xlint:unchecked`, which gives:

Setting.java:12: warning: [unchecked] unchecked cast
        return (T) props.get(key);
                            ^
  required: T
  found:    String
  where T is a type-variable:
    T extends Object declared in method <T>read(Map<String,String>)

After erasure, `T` inside `read` is `Object`, so `(T)` compiles to no check at all. The compiler adds a check (a `checkcast` instruction) in the caller, at the point where the value meets a concrete type, and only when the target needs it: even an explicit `<Integer>` adds no check when the result goes into an `Object`. Where the check lands decides where, or whether, the program fails (`r` is the result of `RETRIES.find(props)`):

Integer retries = RETRIES.read(props)      -> ClassCastException in CallSites.main
String text = RETRIES.read(props)          -> 3 (String)
Object o = RETRIES.<Integer>read(props)    -> 3 (String)
Optional<Integer> r = RETRIES.find(props)  -> Optional[3]
r.isPresent()                              -> true
r.orElse(3) - 1                            -> ClassCastException in CallSites.main
r.map(n -> n * 2)                          -> ClassCastException in Optional.map
r.equals(Optional.of(3))                   -> false

An `Optional<Integer>` holding a `String` is stored without complaint, which is how `RetryPolicy` started cleanly. It fails in the caller's code at `orElse` and inside the JDK at `map`. At `equals`, which takes an `Object`, no check runs at all: it answers `false` and sends a comparison down the wrong branch. None of these places is the enum, so the developer reading the trace starts in the wrong class.
The warning is the one message that points at the cause. Putting `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` on such a method removes it and leaves the bug.
A `Class<T>` Token Makes the Cast Real, Inside the Method
The method can't see `T`, but the caller can hand it over as a `Class<T>` object, a **type token**. `Class.cast` checks at run time, so the check moves into the enum:
It compiles with no warning under `-Xlint:unchecked`. Each constant now parses its own value, and the token decides whether the caller may have it:

RETRIES.read(props, Integer.class)     -> 3 (Integer)
RETRIES.read(props, Number.class)      -> 3 (Integer)
RETRIES.read(props, String.class)      -> ClassCastException: Cannot cast java.lang.Integer to java.lang.String
                                          in Class.cast, called from Setting.read
RETRIES.read(props, int.class)         -> ClassCastException: Cannot cast java.lang.Integer to int
                                          in Class.cast, called from Setting.read
A wrong request now fails on its own line, with both types in the message. `cast` accepts any instance of the token's class, so a supertype such as `Number` works.

`int.class` has the type `Class<Integer>` and so compiles, but no object is an instance of a primitive type, and `int.class.isInstance(3)` is `false`; a method that should accept `int.class` must map it to `Integer.class` first. And a token names a class, not a parameterized type: `List<Integer>.class` doesn't compile, so `Class.cast` can check that a value is a `List` but not what the list holds. A key missing from `props` is no longer an empty `Optional`, either: `HOST.read` returns `null`, since `cast(null)` passes, and `RETRIES.read` throws `NumberFormatException: Cannot parse null string` from its parser.
<!-- practice 1 -->
`E extends Enum<E>` Accepts Any Enum and Hands Back That Enum's Own Type
The JDK's enum utilities all declare the same bound:

public static <T extends Enum<T>> T valueOf(Class<T> enumClass, String name)   // Enum
public static <E extends Enum<E>> EnumSet<E> noneOf(Class<E> elementType)       // EnumSet
public EnumMap(Class<K> keyType)                  // EnumMap<K extends Enum<K>, V>

`Enum` itself is declared `Enum<E extends Enum<E>>`, and the compiler makes an enum `Priority { LOW, NORMAL, HIGH }` extend `Enum<Priority>`. So `E extends Enum<E>` means "an enum type `E`", and a call with any other class doesn't compile:

Bounds.java:7: error: method valueOf in class Enum<E> cannot be applied to given types;
        Enum.valueOf(String.class, "LOW");
            ^
  required: Class<T>,String
  found:    Class<String>,String
  reason: inference variable T has incompatible bounds
    equality constraints: String
    upper bounds: Enum<T>
  where T,E are type-variables:
    T extends Enum<T> declared in method <T>valueOf(Class<T>,String)
    E extends Enum<E> declared in class Enum

The bound also lets `Enum`'s own methods speak in `E`: `compareTo(E)` accepts only constants of the same enum, and `getDeclaringClass()` returns `Class<E>`. A method that moves a status to the next constant uses that:
Spot the Problem: `getClass()` in Place of `getDeclaringClass()`
A colleague writes the same method with `getClass()`. The compiler refuses `E[] all = current.getClass().getEnumConstants()` (`CAP#1[] cannot be converted to E[]`), so they add a cast:
The enum has a constant with a body:

CycleByClass.next(CREATED)                 -> IN_TRANSIT
CycleByClass.next(IN_TRANSIT)              -> java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot read the array length because "all" is null
IN_TRANSIT.getClass()                      -> class Shipment$1
IN_TRANSIT.getClass().getEnumConstants()   -> null
IN_TRANSIT.getDeclaringClass()             -> class Shipment

`IN_TRANSIT` is an instance of an anonymous subclass (unit 7.2.1), and `getEnumConstants()` returns `null` for a class that isn't an enum. The types had said so: `getClass()` returns `Class<? extends Enum>`, which promises nothing about `E`, and the cast hid the compile error that said so. With `getDeclaringClass()`, `next(IN_TRANSIT)` is `DELIVERED`, and `next(DELIVERED)` wraps to `CREATED`.
A Generic `parse` Reads Any Enum Through `getEnumConstants()`
An import reads shipment states and priorities from CSV files, written by people: `in-transit`, ` High `. `Enum.valueOf` matches the exact name only:
Enum.valueOf(Shipment.class, "in-transit") -> java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant Shipment.in-transit
One generic method can do the lenient match for every enum, because `Class<E>` hands over the constants as an `E[]`:

parse(Shipment.class, "in-transit")        -> IN_TRANSIT
parse(Priority.class, " High ")            -> HIGH
parse(Priority.class, "urgent")            -> java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: Priority has no constant for 'urgent'
parseAll(Shipment.class, "delivered,created") -> [CREATED, DELIVERED]
The caller gets a `Shipment` back, with no cast. `EnumSet.noneOf(type)` needs the same `Class<E>` and keeps the constants in declaration order, whatever order the file listed them in.

`getEnumConstants()`, like `values()`, returns a new copy of the array on every call. Calling it for every row of a large file allocates an array per row. A hot path builds a lookup map once per enum (unit 7.2.3).

Summary

items: **An enum can't take a type parameter, but its methods can, and each call picks `T`.** The constant can't promise a type; any caller can ask `RETRIES` for a `String`.
**An unchecked cast checks nothing where it is written.** The value is checked where it meets a concrete type in the caller, or never, so the trace points away from the enum.
**A `Class<T>` token makes the cast real, inside the method.** It fails at the wrong request, but can't express `int` (map it to `Integer`) or `List<Integer>`.
**`E extends Enum<E>` accepts any enum and hands back that enum's own type.** Use `getDeclaringClass()`, which returns `Class<E>`; `getClass()` of a constant with a body isn't an enum class.
**A generic `parse` reads any enum through `getEnumConstants()`.** It returns the caller's own type and pairs with `EnumSet.noneOf(type)`.

blocks.text: Challenges

items: The settings enum grows to forty keys of six types. Compare the `Class<T>` token with a final class of typed keys (unit 7.2.2): what does each catch at compile time, and what does each cost when a key is added?
A library method takes `Class<T>` and you need it to return a `List<Order>`. What can you pass, and where does the unchecked cast end up?
Find the `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` annotations in a codebase you know. For each, which line would the `ClassCastException` point at if the cast were wrong?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why Enum Is Declared `Enum<E extends Enum<E>>`

The self-referencing bound lets methods written once in `Enum` talk about the subclass: `Priority.LOW.compareTo(Shipment.CREATED)` doesn't compile (`Shipment cannot be converted to Priority`), and `EnumSet` and `EnumMap` get the constants of exactly the caller's enum with no cast in the caller's code.

The price is the signatures. `<E extends Enum<E>>` is hard to read, and a reader meeting it in `EnumSet` for the first time has to learn that it only means "an enum". It says nothing about any other type: a setting's value type still needs a token, and a token still can't name `List<Integer>`.
